Refute

rih-FYOOT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To refute to prove that something is false or incorrect.

The debate team's closing argument managed to refute nearly every point their opponents had raised.

Worked Example

Detailed satellite images were enough to refute the company's claim that it had stopped dumping waste into the river.

To refute a claim is to prove, with solid evidence or argument, that it is false -- not just to disagree with it.

How Refute Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disprove

disprove: to show that something is not true

rebut

rebut: to argue against a claim with counter-evidence

Antonyms

confirm

confirm: to establish that something is true

validate

validate: to prove something is well-founded or accurate

How Strong Is It? — question → refute → demolish

question vs. refute

question vs. refute: To question something is simply to raise doubt, without necessarily proving anything false.

demolish vs. refute

demolish vs. refute: To demolish an argument is to completely destroy it, an even more forceful defeat than a careful refutation.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — fute

root — fute: to beat down, to strike (from Latin futare)

Put it together

Put it together: Refute is built from re- ('back') + fute ('to beat down, to strike,' from Latin futare) -- 'to beat back' an argument by proving it false. That root is related to the rare word confute ('to prove wrong') but never became common on its own, so there's no quiz here -- just this one little-known cousin worth knowing about.

Use the root in a new word: confute

Use the root in a new word: confute: The lawyer's precise timeline was enough to confute the witness's entire story, though most people today would simply say 'refute.'

Root Check

Word Choice

Refute means to actually prove something false with evidence or logic -- many people misuse it to mean simply 'deny' or 'disagree with,' but careful writers reserve it for a successful, evidence-backed counter-argument.
